**Remote work**[\[a\]](#cite_note-1) is the practice of [working](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_\(human_activity\) "Work (human activity)") at or from one's [home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home "Home") or [another space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_place "Third place") rather than from an [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office "Office") or workplace.

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries, but remote work for large employers began on a small scale in the 1970s[\[1\]](#cite_note-2) when technology was developed that could link satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). It became more common in the 1990s and 2000s, facilitated by internet technologies such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software") on [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") and [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call") via [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"). In 2020, workplace hazard controls during the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a rapid transition to remote work for white-collar workers around the world. This shift largely persisted even after restrictions were lifted.

Proponents of a geographically distributed workforce argue that it reduces costs associated with maintaining an office, grants employees greater autonomy and flexibility—which improves their motivation and job satisfaction—eliminates environmental harms from commuting, allows employers to access a more geographically diverse pool of applicants, and enables employees to live where they prefer.[\[2\]](#cite_note-3)

Opponents of remote work argue that remote telecommunications technology has been unable to fully replicate the advantages of face-to-face interaction, that employees may be more easily distracted, and that reduced social interaction may lead to feelings of isolation.

## History

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")\]

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries. Management had to rely on trust and control to successfully manage distributed work. In addition to dispersed operations that relied heavily on a combination of explicit information and detailed record-keeping, more tacit and situated knowledge developed through socialization. For example, the [Hudson's Bay Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company "Hudson's Bay Company") showed a variety of control mechanisms including selection techniques, information requirements, and direct local oversight through its distributed practices of [socialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialization "Socialization"), [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication"), and participation. Managers found that "common sense" was not enough to encourage everyone to comply.[\[3\]](#cite_note-4)

The [England and Wales census of 1911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_United_Kingdom_census "1911 United Kingdom census") included a question about each resident person's employment (if any) and included a question about whether they worked "at home".[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)

In the early 1970s, technology was developed that linked satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). The terms *telecommuting* and *telework* were coined by Jack Nilles in 1973.[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)[\[6\]](#cite_note-7) By 1984 a [United Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Technologies "United Technologies") programmer lived in Washington state and telecommuted to his Connecticut office, and the company estimated that executives with computers at home did another two hours of work there.[\[7\]](#cite_note-somerson19840417-8) In January 1986, Erik Sandberg Diment of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported in his weekly column that "As one of the seemingly few people to be actively engaged in telecommuting", he had only visited his office twice in the previous year.[\[8\]](#cite_note-esd19860121-9) In 1979, five [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") employees were allowed to work from home as an experiment. By 1983, the experiment was expanded to 2,000 people. By the early 1980s, branch offices and home workers were able to connect to organizational mainframes using [personal computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") and [terminal emulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_emulator "Terminal emulator").

In 1995, the [motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto "Motto") that "work is something you do, not something you travel to" was coined.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Variations of this motto include: "Work is what we do, not where we are."[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

Since the 1980s, the normalization of remote work has been on a steady incline. For example, the number of Americans working from home grew by 4 million from 2003 to 2006,[\[11\]](#cite_note-gajendran2007-12) and by 1983 academics were beginning to experiment with online conferencing.[\[12\]](#cite_note-byrd2021-13)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

In the 1990s and 2000s, remote work became facilitated by technology such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software"), [virtual private networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_private_network "Virtual private network"), [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call"), [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"), [internet access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_access "Internet access"), [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"), [voice over IP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_over_IP "Voice over IP") (VoIP), [mobile telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_telecommunication "Mobile telecommunication") technology such as a [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi")\-equipped [laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") or [tablet computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer"), [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone"), and [desktop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_computer "Desktop computer"), using software such as [Zoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_\(software\) "Zoom (software)"), [Webex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco_Webex "Cisco Webex"), [Microsoft Teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Teams "Microsoft Teams"), [Google Meet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Meet "Google Meet"), [Slack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_\(software\) "Slack (software)"), and [WhatsApp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WhatsApp "WhatsApp"). Remote-first companies have also experimented with consumer messaging platforms to strengthen workplace culture. For example, CRM company [Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_\(company\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Close (company) (page does not exist)") has used [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") internally to encourage informal communication among distributed employees.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

In his 1992 travelogue *Exploring the Internet*, [Carl Malamud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Malamud "Carl Malamud") described a "[digital nomad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad "Digital nomad")" as a person who "travels the world with a laptop, setting up [FidoNet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FidoNet "FidoNet") [nodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_\(networking\) "Node (networking)")."[\[14\]](#cite_note-15) In 1993, [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") published the *Digital Nomad's Guide* series of guidebooks by Mitch Ratcliffe and Andrew Gore. The guidebooks, *PowerBook*, *AT&T EO Personal Communicator*, and *Newton's Law*, used the term "digital nomad" to refer to the increased mobility and more powerful communication and productivity technologies that facilitated remote work.[\[15\]](#cite_note-16)[\[16\]](#cite_note-17)[\[17\]](#cite_note-18)

European [hacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacker "Hacker") spaces of the 1990s led to [coworking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coworking "Coworking"); the first such space opened in 2005.[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) The new economy production no longer requires people to work together in the same physical space to access the tools and resources they need to produce their work and allows for distributed work.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)

In 2010, the Telework Enhancement Act of 2010 required each [executive agency in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federal_agencies_in_the_United_States "List of federal agencies in the United States") to establish policy allowing remote work to the maximum extent possible, so long as employee performance is not diminished.[\[20\]](#cite_note-21)[\[21\]](#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](#cite_note-23)

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), millions of workers began working remotely for the first time.[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) Cities in which the population of remote workers increased significantly were referred to as [Zoom towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_town "Zoom town").[\[24\]](#cite_note-25) According to a [U.S. Labor Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Labor_Department "U.S. Labor Department") study published, millions of Americans ceased working from home by 2022, and the number of employers reporting teleworking decreased to the level before pandemic levels. From August to September 2022, approximately 72 percent of private-sector businesses reported little to no telework among workers, compared to roughly 60 percent from July to September 2021.[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) During the [Information Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age"), many [startups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startups "Startups") were founded in the homes of entrepreneurs who lacked financial resources.[\[26\]](#cite_note-27)

### Remote work during COVID-19

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Remote work during COVID-19")\]

A 2020 study of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") estimated that 93% of world workers lived in countries with some sort of workplace closure. This figure was composed of: 32% living in countries with required closures for *all* but essential workplaces; 42% in countries where specific firms or worker categories had been closed; and 19% in countries with only recommended workplace closures.[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)

The extensive use of remote work under COVID-19 constituted a major organizational transformation. However, the implementation of remote work during COVID-19 was hurried, and new technologies and operating systems had to be implemented without previous testing or training.[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) Organizations reported concerns about losses in culture and productivity whilst workers were more concerned about declines in social interactions,[\[29\]](#cite_note-Majumdar20-30) internet connectivity and increased workload.[\[30\]](#cite_note-31) Additionally, 25% of remote-working Americans were resistant to employer mandates to return to in-office work.[\[31\]](#cite_note-32) Especially after the end of the pandemic, many businesses tried to recall their workforce to the office.[\[32\]](#cite_note-33)[\[33\]](#cite_note-34)[\[34\]](#cite_note-35)[\[35\]](#cite_note-36)

The abrupt transition to remote work during the pandemic led to an increase in both physical and mental health issues among workers; distractions from others in the home and a lack of dedicated workspaces were common negative influences on health and well-being, while effective communication with coworkers was supportive of health and well-being.[\[36\]](#cite_note-37) The transition also increased the amount of time that individuals spent sitting at a workstation by up to two hours more per day, yet, most workers indicated being as productive working remotely as compared to office work before the pandemic.[\[37\]](#cite_note-38) Supporting workers to identify effective approaches for boundary management between home and work across physical spaces, social interactions, and the use of time is critical.[\[38\]](#cite_note-39) Research suggests that remote work can lead to increased employee satisfaction and productivity, but may also create challenges in team cohesion.[\[39\]](#cite_note-40)

The transition to remote work during the pandemic highlighted the importance of access and equity among individual workers to support productivity and well-being. The remote work arrangement during COVID-19 was better for higher-paid and higher-management personnel in terms of productivity and reported well-being; whereas individuals at the bottom end of the earning spectrum experienced reduced remuneration.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41) Utility bills also increased during the COVID-19 pandemic in an inconsistent manner. Utility bills for minorities and lower income individuals were more likely to increase because they lived in housing that was older, with less effective [insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_insulation "Building insulation") and without [energy-efficient appliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficient_energy_use#Appliances "Efficient energy use"). The increase in electricity also came due to the people using their utilities at different times of the day.[\[41\]](#cite_note-42)

A 2024 [PNAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNAS "PNAS") study found that remote work dispersed economic activity away from city centers, in particular in cities with high levels of remote work.[\[42\]](#cite_note-43)

### United States

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: United States")\]

The U.S. Census Bureau estimated that 13.8 percent of U.S. workers, more than 22 million people, usually worked from home in 2023. The share was down from 17.9 percent in 2021 and 15.2 percent in 2022, but remained more than twice the 5.7 percent recorded in 2019.[\[46\]](#cite_note-47)

According to a Gallup poll in September 2021, 45% of full-time U.S. employees worked from home, including 25% who worked from home full-time and 20% who worked from home part-time. Ninety-one percent of those who worked remotely (fully or partially) hoped to continue doing so after the pandemic. Among all workers, 54% believed that their company's culture would be unchanged by remote work, while 12% believed it would improve and 33% predicted it would deteriorate.[\[47\]](#cite_note-gallup2021-48)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

Gallup found in February 2023 that, among remote-capable employees in the U.S., 20% worked on-site, 28% exclusively remote and 52% hybrid.[\[48\]](#cite_note-49)

According to the [United States Office of Personnel Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Personnel_Management "United States Office of Personnel Management"), 50% of all U.S. federal workers were eligible to work remotely and agencies saved more than $180 million because of remote work in fiscal 2020.[\[49\]](#cite_note-50)

A September 2022 study[\[b\]](#cite_note-51) surveyed workers in mid-2021 and early 2022. Its 2,079 US subjects worked from home on average 1.6 days per week, similar to the global average of 1.5 days per week.[\[50\]](#cite_note-:1-52)

### Communication technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Communication technology")\]

Effective group communication involves various nonverbal communication characteristics. Because distance limits interpersonal interaction between members of [distributed groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_team?action=edit&redlink=1 "Distributed team (page does not exist)"), these characteristics often become constrained. [Communication media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_media "Communication media") focuses on alternative ways to achieve these qualities and promote effective communication. This section addresses [communication technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_technology "Communication technology") in relation to the theories of [grounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_\(communication\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grounding (communication) (page does not exist)") and [mutual knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_knowledge "Common knowledge") and discusses the costs and benefits of various communication technology tools..

#### Grounding and technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Grounding and technology")\]

[Grounding in communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_in_communication "Grounding in communication") is the process of updating the evolving common ground, or shared information, between participants. The base of mutual knowledge is important for effective coordination and communication.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64) Additionally, participants constantly gather various forms of verbal and nonverbal evidence to establish understanding of change and task.

The following are means of grounding and collecting evidence:

Quality

Description

Co-presence

When sharing the same physical environment, participants are able to easily and hear what the other is doing and looking at.

Visibility

The participants are able to see each other and are able to pick up non-verbal facial cues and body language.

Audibility

When the participants are able to communicate by speaking, they are able to pick up voice intonation and utterance timing.

Cotemporality

Efficiency is promoted when an utterance is produced just about when it is received and understood, without delay.

Simultaneity

Messages can be simultaneously conveyed and received by both participants.

Sequentiality

The participants speak only with each other without intervening turns from conversations with other people.

Reviewability

Participants are able to return to a physical form of the exchange at a later time.

Revisability

Participants are able to privately revise their statements before sending their message.

Different forms of [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication") result in the varied presence of these communication characteristics. Therefore, the nature of communication technology can either promote or inhibit grounding between participants. The absence of grounding information results in reduced ability to read and understand social cues. This increases the social distance between them.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64)

#### Costs to grounding change

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Costs to grounding change")\]

There is often a trade-off between the costs: one cost will increase as another decreases. There is also often a [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation "Correlation") between the costs. ## Legal aspects

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legal aspects")\]

In 1996, the [Home Work Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Work_Convention "Home Work Convention"), an [International Labour Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Labour_Organization "International Labour Organization") (ILO) [Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty"), was created to offer protection to workers who are employed in their own homes.

The UK's [National Minimum Wage Act 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Minimum_Wage_Act_1998 "National Minimum Wage Act 1998") makes specific reference to home workers who "contract with a person, for the purposes of that person's business, for the execution of work to be done in a place not under the control or management of that person".[\[61\]](#cite_note-65) In the case of [James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_v_Redcats_\(Brands\)_Ltd "James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd") (2007), it was confirmed that "a home worker need not work at home, although typically he or she will do so; the only requirement is to work in a place not under the control or management of the other party".[\[62\]](#cite_note-66)

In the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), the Flexible Working Act allows workers to submit a written request to work from home, at least partly. Employers must have a good reason for refusing worker requests.[\[63\]](#cite_note-67)

## Potential benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Potential benefits")\]

### Disability employment

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Disability employment")\]

A 2026 study in the *[American Economic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Economic_Review "American Economic Review")* found that the expansion of remote work has led to a substantial increase in disability employment by reducing the commuting costs of physically disabled workers and allowing them to better control their work conditions to suit their disabilities.[\[64\]](#cite_note-aer2026-68)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

### Access to more employees/employers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Access to more employees/employers")\]

Remote work allows employees and employers to be matched despite major location differences.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

Working responsibility is given to the employee who is skilled in that area of work.[\[66\]](#cite_note-Hunter-2019-70)

### Cost reduction

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Cost reduction")\]

Remote work can [reduce costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_reduction "Cost reduction") for organizations, including the cost of office space and related expenses such as parking, computer equipment, furniture, [office supplies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_supplies "Office supplies"), lighting and [heating, ventilation, and air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heating,_ventilation,_and_air_conditioning "Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning").[\[67\]](#cite_note-profits-71) Certain employee expenses, such as office expenses, can be shifted to the remote worker, although this is the subject of lawsuits.[\[68\]](#cite_note-72)

Remote work also reduces costs for the worker such as costs of travel/[commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting")[\[69\]](#cite_note-73)[\[70\]](#cite_note-impact-74) and clothing.[\[71\]](#cite_note-75) It also allows for the possibility of living in a cheaper area than that of the office.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

### Environmental benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environmental benefits")\]

See also: [Mobility transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobility_transition "Mobility transition")

Remote work can reduce [traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion "Traffic congestion") and [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution "Air pollution"), with fewer cars on the roads.

Most studies find that remote work overall results in a decrease in energy use due to less time spent on energy-intensive personal transportation,[\[72\]](#cite_note-76) cleaner air,[\[73\]](#cite_note-77) and a reduction of electricity usage due to a lower office space footprint.[\[74\]](#cite_note-78)

During the [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns"), the increase in remote work led to a decrease in global [CO2 emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CO2_emissions "CO2 emissions").[\[75\]](#cite_note-79) Partially due to the decrease in car commuting, carbon emissions dropped by 5.4%; however, emissions immediately increased to the same rate in the following year.[\[76\]](#cite_note-80)

The increase in remote work had also led to people moving out of cities and into larger homes which catered for home office space.[\[77\]](#cite_note-81)

### Fewer disruptions and distractions

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Fewer disruptions and distractions")\]

Empirical studies find fewer in-office interruptions as a mechanism for productivity gains in remote or hybrid arrangements, particularly for knowledge-based work and concentration-heavy tasks. These include ambient noise such as background chatter and noise from machinery, and forced disruptions such as meetings and check-ins that an on-site employee would not have control over. Remote work gives employees flexibility and control over their environment in regard to distractions.

A 2024 study published by the *[Journal of Business and Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Business_and_Psychology "Journal of Business and Psychology")* found that there was a positive effect on daily job performance when working remotely, mediated by higher concentration and greater work engagement.[\[78\]](#cite_note-82) A 2025 study published by *[Computers in Human Behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computers_in_Human_Behavior "Computers in Human Behavior")* found that working from home increased job concentration; in particular, among those with stable personality traits, the negative effects of increased social isolation were buffered.[\[79\]](#cite_note-83)

**Remote work**[\[a\]](#cite_note-1) is the practice of [working](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_\(human_activity\) "Work (human activity)") at or from one's [home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home "Home") or [another space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_place "Third place") rather than from an [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office "Office") or workplace.

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries, but remote work for large employers began on a small scale in the 1970s[\[1\]](#cite_note-2) when technology was developed that could link satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). It became more common in the 1990s and 2000s, facilitated by internet technologies such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software") on [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") and [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call") via [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"). In 2020, workplace hazard controls during the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a rapid transition to remote work for white-collar workers around the world. This shift largely persisted even after restrictions were lifted.

Proponents of a geographically distributed workforce argue that it reduces costs associated with maintaining an office, grants employees greater autonomy and flexibility—which improves their motivation and job satisfaction—eliminates environmental harms from commuting, allows employers to access a more geographically diverse pool of applicants, and enables employees to live where they prefer.[\[2\]](#cite_note-3)

Opponents of remote work argue that remote telecommunications technology has been unable to fully replicate the advantages of face-to-face interaction, that employees may be more easily distracted, and that reduced social interaction may lead to feelings of isolation.

## History

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")\]

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries. Management had to rely on trust and control to successfully manage distributed work. In addition to dispersed operations that relied heavily on a combination of explicit information and detailed record-keeping, more tacit and situated knowledge developed through socialization. For example, the [Hudson's Bay Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company "Hudson's Bay Company") showed a variety of control mechanisms including selection techniques, information requirements, and direct local oversight through its distributed practices of [socialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialization "Socialization"), [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication"), and participation. Managers found that "common sense" was not enough to encourage everyone to comply.[\[3\]](#cite_note-4)

The [England and Wales census of 1911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_United_Kingdom_census "1911 United Kingdom census") included a question about each resident person's employment (if any) and included a question about whether they worked "at home".[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)

In the early 1970s, technology was developed that linked satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). The terms *telecommuting* and *telework* were coined by Jack Nilles in 1973.[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)[\[6\]](#cite_note-7) By 1984 a [United Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Technologies "United Technologies") programmer lived in Washington state and telecommuted to his Connecticut office, and the company estimated that executives with computers at home did another two hours of work there.[\[7\]](#cite_note-somerson19840417-8) In January 1986, Erik Sandberg Diment of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported in his weekly column that "As one of the seemingly few people to be actively engaged in telecommuting", he had only visited his office twice in the previous year.[\[8\]](#cite_note-esd19860121-9) In 1979, five [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") employees were allowed to work from home as an experiment. By 1983, the experiment was expanded to 2,000 people. By the early 1980s, branch offices and home workers were able to connect to organizational mainframes using [personal computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") and [terminal emulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_emulator "Terminal emulator").

In 1995, the [motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto "Motto") that "work is something you do, not something you travel to" was coined.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Variations of this motto include: "Work is what we do, not where we are."[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

Since the 1980s, the normalization of remote work has been on a steady incline. For example, the number of Americans working from home grew by 4 million from 2003 to 2006,[\[11\]](#cite_note-gajendran2007-12) and by 1983 academics were beginning to experiment with online conferencing.[\[12\]](#cite_note-byrd2021-13)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

In the 1990s and 2000s, remote work became facilitated by technology such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software"), [virtual private networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_private_network "Virtual private network"), [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call"), [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"), [internet access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_access "Internet access"), [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"), [voice over IP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_over_IP "Voice over IP") (VoIP), [mobile telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_telecommunication "Mobile telecommunication") technology such as a [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi")\-equipped [laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") or [tablet computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer"), [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone"), and [desktop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_computer "Desktop computer"), using software such as [Zoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_\(software\) "Zoom (software)"), [Webex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco_Webex "Cisco Webex"), [Microsoft Teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Teams "Microsoft Teams"), [Google Meet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Meet "Google Meet"), [Slack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_\(software\) "Slack (software)"), and [WhatsApp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WhatsApp "WhatsApp"). Remote-first companies have also experimented with consumer messaging platforms to strengthen workplace culture. For example, CRM company [Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_\(company\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Close (company) (page does not exist)") has used [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") internally to encourage informal communication among distributed employees.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

In his 1992 travelogue *Exploring the Internet*, [Carl Malamud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Malamud "Carl Malamud") described a "[digital nomad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad "Digital nomad")" as a person who "travels the world with a laptop, setting up [FidoNet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FidoNet "FidoNet") [nodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_\(networking\) "Node (networking)")."[\[14\]](#cite_note-15) In 1993, [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") published the *Digital Nomad's Guide* series of guidebooks by Mitch Ratcliffe and Andrew Gore. The guidebooks, *PowerBook*, *AT&T EO Personal Communicator*, and *Newton's Law*, used the term "digital nomad" to refer to the increased mobility and more powerful communication and productivity technologies that facilitated remote work.[\[15\]](#cite_note-16)[\[16\]](#cite_note-17)[\[17\]](#cite_note-18)

European [hacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacker "Hacker") spaces of the 1990s led to [coworking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coworking "Coworking"); the first such space opened in 2005.[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) The new economy production no longer requires people to work together in the same physical space to access the tools and resources they need to produce their work and allows for distributed work.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)

In 2010, the Telework Enhancement Act of 2010 required each [executive agency in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federal_agencies_in_the_United_States "List of federal agencies in the United States") to establish policy allowing remote work to the maximum extent possible, so long as employee performance is not diminished.[\[20\]](#cite_note-21)[\[21\]](#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](#cite_note-23)

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), millions of workers began working remotely for the first time.[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) Cities in which the population of remote workers increased significantly were referred to as [Zoom towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_town "Zoom town").[\[24\]](#cite_note-25) According to a [U.S. Labor Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Labor_Department "U.S. Labor Department") study published, millions of Americans ceased working from home by 2022, and the number of employers reporting teleworking decreased to the level before pandemic levels. From August to September 2022, approximately 72 percent of private-sector businesses reported little to no telework among workers, compared to roughly 60 percent from July to September 2021.[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) During the [Information Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age"), many [startups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startups "Startups") were founded in the homes of entrepreneurs who lacked financial resources.[\[26\]](#cite_note-27)

### Remote work during COVID-19

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Remote work during COVID-19")\]

A 2020 study of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") estimated that 93% of world workers lived in countries with some sort of workplace closure. This figure was composed of: 32% living in countries with required closures for *all* but essential workplaces; 42% in countries where specific firms or worker categories had been closed; and 19% in countries with only recommended workplace closures.[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)

The extensive use of remote work under COVID-19 constituted a major organizational transformation. However, the implementation of remote work during COVID-19 was hurried, and new technologies and operating systems had to be implemented without previous testing or training.[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) Organizations reported concerns about losses in culture and productivity whilst workers were more concerned about declines in social interactions,[\[29\]](#cite_note-Majumdar20-30) internet connectivity and increased workload.[\[30\]](#cite_note-31) Additionally, 25% of remote-working Americans were resistant to employer mandates to return to in-office work.[\[31\]](#cite_note-32) Especially after the end of the pandemic, many businesses tried to recall their workforce to the office.[\[32\]](#cite_note-33)[\[33\]](#cite_note-34)[\[34\]](#cite_note-35)[\[35\]](#cite_note-36)

The abrupt transition to remote work during the pandemic led to an increase in both physical and mental health issues among workers; distractions from others in the home and a lack of dedicated workspaces were common negative influences on health and well-being, while effective communication with coworkers was supportive of health and well-being.[\[36\]](#cite_note-37) The transition also increased the amount of time that individuals spent sitting at a workstation by up to two hours more per day, yet, most workers indicated being as productive working remotely as compared to office work before the pandemic.[\[37\]](#cite_note-38) Supporting workers to identify effective approaches for boundary management between home and work across physical spaces, social interactions, and the use of time is critical.[\[38\]](#cite_note-39) Research suggests that remote work can lead to increased employee satisfaction and productivity, but may also create challenges in team cohesion.[\[39\]](#cite_note-40)

The transition to remote work during the pandemic highlighted the importance of access and equity among individual workers to support productivity and well-being. The remote work arrangement during COVID-19 was better for higher-paid and higher-management personnel in terms of productivity and reported well-being; whereas individuals at the bottom end of the earning spectrum experienced reduced remuneration.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41) Utility bills also increased during the COVID-19 pandemic in an inconsistent manner. Utility bills for minorities and lower income individuals were more likely to increase because they lived in housing that was older, with less effective [insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_insulation "Building insulation") and without [energy-efficient appliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficient_energy_use#Appliances "Efficient energy use"). The increase in electricity also came due to the people using their utilities at different times of the day.[\[41\]](#cite_note-42)

A 2024 [PNAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNAS "PNAS") study found that remote work dispersed economic activity away from city centers, in particular in cities with high levels of remote work.[\[42\]](#cite_note-43)

### Communication technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Communication technology")\]

Effective group communication involves various nonverbal communication characteristics. Because distance limits interpersonal interaction between members of [distributed groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_team?action=edit&redlink=1 "Distributed team (page does not exist)"), these characteristics often become constrained. [Communication media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_media "Communication media") focuses on alternative ways to achieve these qualities and promote effective communication. This section addresses [communication technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_technology "Communication technology") in relation to the theories of [grounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_\(communication\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grounding (communication) (page does not exist)") and [mutual knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_knowledge "Common knowledge") and discusses the costs and benefits of various communication technology tools..

#### Grounding and technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Grounding and technology")\]

[Grounding in communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_in_communication "Grounding in communication") is the process of updating the evolving common ground, or shared information, between participants. The base of mutual knowledge is important for effective coordination and communication.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64) Additionally, participants constantly gather various forms of verbal and nonverbal evidence to establish understanding of change and task.

The following are means of grounding and collecting evidence:

Quality

Description

Co-presence

When sharing the same physical environment, participants are able to easily and hear what the other is doing and looking at.

Visibility

The participants are able to see each other and are able to pick up non-verbal facial cues and body language.

Audibility

When the participants are able to communicate by speaking, they are able to pick up voice intonation and utterance timing.

Cotemporality

Efficiency is promoted when an utterance is produced just about when it is received and understood, without delay.

Simultaneity

Messages can be simultaneously conveyed and received by both participants.

Sequentiality

The participants speak only with each other without intervening turns from conversations with other people.

Reviewability

Participants are able to return to a physical form of the exchange at a later time.

Revisability

Participants are able to privately revise their statements before sending their message.

Different forms of [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication") result in the varied presence of these communication characteristics. Therefore, the nature of communication technology can either promote or inhibit grounding between participants. The absence of grounding information results in reduced ability to read and understand social cues. This increases the social distance between them.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64)

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Costs to grounding change")\]

There is also often a [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation "Correlation") between the costs. ## Legal aspects

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legal aspects")\]

In 1996, the [Home Work Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Work_Convention "Home Work Convention"), an [International Labour Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Labour_Organization "International Labour Organization") (ILO) [Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty"), was created to offer protection to workers who are employed in their own homes.

The UK's [National Minimum Wage Act 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Minimum_Wage_Act_1998 "National Minimum Wage Act 1998") makes specific reference to home workers who "contract with a person, for the purposes of that person's business, for the execution of work to be done in a place not under the control or management of that person".[\[61\]](#cite_note-65) In the case of [James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_v_Redcats_\(Brands\)_Ltd "James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd") (2007), it was confirmed that "a home worker need not work at home, although typically he or she will do so; the only requirement is to work in a place not under the control or management of the other party".[\[62\]](#cite_note-66)

In the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), the Flexible Working Act allows workers to submit a written request to work from home, at least partly. Employers must have a good reason for refusing worker requests.[\[63\]](#cite_note-67)

## Potential benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Potential benefits")\]

### Disability employment

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Disability employment")\]

A 2026 study in the *[American Economic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Economic_Review "American Economic Review")* found that the expansion of remote work has led to a substantial increase in disability employment by reducing the commuting costs of physically disabled workers and allowing them to better control their work conditions to suit their disabilities.[\[64\]](#cite_note-aer2026-68)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

### Access to more employees/employers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Access to more employees/employers")\]

Remote work allows employees and employers to be matched despite major location differences.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

Working responsibility is given to the employee who is skilled in that area of work.[\[66\]](#cite_note-Hunter-2019-70)

### Cost reduction

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Cost reduction")\]

Remote work can [reduce costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_reduction "Cost reduction") for organizations, including the cost of office space and related expenses such as parking, computer equipment, furniture, [office supplies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_supplies "Office supplies"), lighting and [heating, ventilation, and air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heating,_ventilation,_and_air_conditioning "Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning").[\[67\]](#cite_note-profits-71) Certain employee expenses, such as office expenses, can be shifted to the remote worker, although this is the subject of lawsuits.[\[68\]](#cite_note-72)

Remote work also reduces costs for the worker such as costs of travel/[commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting")[\[69\]](#cite_note-73)[\[70\]](#cite_note-impact-74) and clothing.[\[71\]](#cite_note-75) It also allows for the possibility of living in a cheaper area than that of the office.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

### Environmental benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environmental benefits")\]

See also: [Mobility transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobility_transition "Mobility transition")

Remote work can reduce [traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion "Traffic congestion") and [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution "Air pollution"), with fewer cars on the roads.

Most studies find that remote work overall results in a decrease in energy use due to less time spent on energy-intensive personal transportation,[\[72\]](#cite_note-76) cleaner air,[\[73\]](#cite_note-77) and a reduction of electricity usage due to a lower office space footprint.[\[74\]](#cite_note-78)

During the [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns"), the increase in remote work led to a decrease in global [CO2 emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CO2_emissions "CO2 emissions").[\[75\]](#cite_note-79) Partially due to the decrease in car commuting, carbon emissions dropped by 5.4%; however, emissions immediately increased to the same rate in the following year.[\[76\]](#cite_note-80)

The increase in remote work had also led to people moving out of cities and into larger homes which catered for home office space.[\[77\]](#cite_note-81)

### Fewer disruptions and distractions

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Fewer disruptions and distractions")\]

Empirical studies find fewer in-office interruptions as a mechanism for productivity gains in remote or hybrid arrangements, particularly for knowledge-based work and concentration-heavy tasks. These include ambient noise such as background chatter and noise from machinery, and forced disruptions such as meetings and check-ins that an on-site employee would not have control over. Remote work gives employees flexibility and control over their environment in regard to distractions.

A 2024 study published by the *[Journal of Business and Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Business_and_Psychology "Journal of Business and Psychology")* found that there was a positive effect on daily job performance when working remotely, mediated by higher concentration and greater work engagement.[\[78\]](#cite_note-82) A 2025 study published by *[Computers in Human Behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computers_in_Human_Behavior "Computers in Human Behavior")* found that working from home increased job concentration; in particular, among those with stable personality traits, the negative effects of increased social isolation were buffered.[\[79\]](#cite_note-83)

The [United States Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") began allowing remote work in 2010.

**Remote work**[\[a\]](#cite_note-1) is the practice of [working](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_\(human_activity\) "Work (human activity)") at or from one's [home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home "Home") or [another space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_place "Third place") rather than from an [office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office "Office") or workplace.

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries, but remote work for large employers began on a small scale in the 1970s[\[1\]](#cite_note-2) when technology was developed that could link satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). It became more common in the 1990s and 2000s, facilitated by internet technologies such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software") on [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") and [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call") via [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"). In 2020, workplace hazard controls during the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a rapid transition to remote work for white-collar workers around the world. This shift largely persisted even after restrictions were lifted.

Proponents of a geographically distributed workforce argue that it reduces costs associated with maintaining an office, grants employees greater autonomy and flexibility—which improves their motivation and job satisfaction—eliminates environmental harms from commuting, allows employers to access a more geographically diverse pool of applicants, and enables employees to live where they prefer.[\[2\]](#cite_note-3)

Opponents of remote work argue that remote telecommunications technology has been unable to fully replicate the advantages of face-to-face interaction, that employees may be more easily distracted, and that reduced social interaction may lead to feelings of isolation.

## History

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")\]

The practice of working at home has been documented for centuries. Management had to rely on trust and control to successfully manage distributed work. In addition to dispersed operations that relied heavily on a combination of explicit information and detailed record-keeping, more tacit and situated knowledge developed through socialization. For example, the [Hudson's Bay Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company "Hudson's Bay Company") showed a variety of control mechanisms including selection techniques, information requirements, and direct local oversight through its distributed practices of [socialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialization "Socialization"), [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication"), and participation. Managers found that "common sense" was not enough to encourage everyone to comply.[\[3\]](#cite_note-4)

The [England and Wales census of 1911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_United_Kingdom_census "1911 United Kingdom census") included a question about each resident person's employment (if any) and included a question about whether they worked "at home".[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)

In the early 1970s, technology was developed that linked satellite offices to downtown mainframes through [dumb terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumb_terminal "Dumb terminal") using telephone lines as a [network bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_bridge "Network bridge"). The terms *telecommuting* and *telework* were coined by Jack Nilles in 1973.[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)[\[6\]](#cite_note-7) By 1984 a [United Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Technologies "United Technologies") programmer lived in Washington state and telecommuted to his Connecticut office, and the company estimated that executives with computers at home did another two hours of work there.[\[7\]](#cite_note-somerson19840417-8) In January 1986, Erik Sandberg Diment of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported in his weekly column that "As one of the seemingly few people to be actively engaged in telecommuting", he had only visited his office twice in the previous year.[\[8\]](#cite_note-esd19860121-9) In 1979, five [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") employees were allowed to work from home as an experiment. By 1983, the experiment was expanded to 2,000 people. By the early 1980s, branch offices and home workers were able to connect to organizational mainframes using [personal computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") and [terminal emulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_emulator "Terminal emulator").

In 1995, the [motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto "Motto") that "work is something you do, not something you travel to" was coined.[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) Variations of this motto include: "Work is what we do, not where we are."[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

Since the 1980s, the normalization of remote work has been on a steady incline. For example, the number of Americans working from home grew by 4 million from 2003 to 2006,[\[11\]](#cite_note-gajendran2007-12) and by 1983 academics were beginning to experiment with online conferencing.[\[12\]](#cite_note-byrd2021-13)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

In the 1990s and 2000s, remote work became facilitated by technology such as [collaborative software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_software "Collaborative software"), [virtual private networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_private_network "Virtual private network"), [conference calling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_call "Conference call"), [videotelephony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotelephony "Videotelephony"), [internet access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_access "Internet access"), [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"), [voice over IP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_over_IP "Voice over IP") (VoIP), [mobile telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_telecommunication "Mobile telecommunication") technology such as a [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi")\-equipped [laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") or [tablet computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer"), [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone"), and [desktop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_computer "Desktop computer"), using software such as [Zoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_\(software\) "Zoom (software)"), [Webex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisco_Webex "Cisco Webex"), [Microsoft Teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Teams "Microsoft Teams"), [Google Meet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Meet "Google Meet"), [Slack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_\(software\) "Slack (software)"), and [WhatsApp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WhatsApp "WhatsApp"). Remote-first companies have also experimented with consumer messaging platforms to strengthen workplace culture. For example, CRM company [Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_\(company\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Close (company) (page does not exist)") has used [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat") internally to encourage informal communication among distributed employees.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

In his 1992 travelogue *Exploring the Internet*, [Carl Malamud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Malamud "Carl Malamud") described a "[digital nomad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad "Digital nomad")" as a person who "travels the world with a laptop, setting up [FidoNet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FidoNet "FidoNet") [nodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_\(networking\) "Node (networking)")."[\[14\]](#cite_note-15) In 1993, [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") published the *Digital Nomad's Guide* series of guidebooks by Mitch Ratcliffe and Andrew Gore. The guidebooks, *PowerBook*, *AT&T EO Personal Communicator*, and *Newton's Law*, used the term "digital nomad" to refer to the increased mobility and more powerful communication and productivity technologies that facilitated remote work.[\[15\]](#cite_note-16)[\[16\]](#cite_note-17)[\[17\]](#cite_note-18)

European [hacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacker "Hacker") spaces of the 1990s led to [coworking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coworking "Coworking"); the first such space opened in 2005.[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) The new economy production no longer requires people to work together in the same physical space to access the tools and resources they need to produce their work and allows for distributed work.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20)

In 2010, the Telework Enhancement Act of 2010 required each [executive agency in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federal_agencies_in_the_United_States "List of federal agencies in the United States") to establish policy allowing remote work to the maximum extent possible, so long as employee performance is not diminished.[\[20\]](#cite_note-21)[\[21\]](#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](#cite_note-23)

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), millions of workers began working remotely for the first time.[\[23\]](#cite_note-24) Cities in which the population of remote workers increased significantly were referred to as [Zoom towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_town "Zoom town").[\[24\]](#cite_note-25) According to a [U.S. Labor Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Labor_Department "U.S. Labor Department") study published, millions of Americans ceased working from home by 2022, and the number of employers reporting teleworking decreased to the level before pandemic levels. From August to September 2022, approximately 72 percent of private-sector businesses reported little to no telework among workers, compared to roughly 60 percent from July to September 2021.[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) During the [Information Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Age "Information Age"), many [startups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startups "Startups") were founded in the homes of entrepreneurs who lacked financial resources.[\[26\]](#cite_note-27)

### Remote work during COVID-19

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Remote work during COVID-19")\]

A 2020 study of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") estimated that 93% of world workers lived in countries with some sort of workplace closure. This figure was composed of: 32% living in countries with required closures for *all* but essential workplaces; 42% in countries where specific firms or worker categories had been closed; and 19% in countries with only recommended workplace closures.[\[27\]](#cite_note-28)

The extensive use of remote work under COVID-19 constituted a major organizational transformation. However, the implementation of remote work during COVID-19 was hurried, and new technologies and operating systems had to be implemented without previous testing or training.[\[28\]](#cite_note-29) Organizations reported concerns about losses in culture and productivity whilst workers were more concerned about declines in social interactions,[\[29\]](#cite_note-Majumdar20-30) internet connectivity and increased workload.[\[30\]](#cite_note-31) Additionally, 25% of remote-working Americans were resistant to employer mandates to return to in-office work.[\[31\]](#cite_note-32) Especially after the end of the pandemic, many businesses tried to recall their workforce to the office.[\[32\]](#cite_note-33)[\[33\]](#cite_note-34)[\[34\]](#cite_note-35)[\[35\]](#cite_note-36)

The abrupt transition to remote work during the pandemic led to an increase in both physical and mental health issues among workers; distractions from others in the home and a lack of dedicated workspaces were common negative influences on health and well-being, while effective communication with coworkers was supportive of health and well-being.[\[36\]](#cite_note-37) The transition also increased the amount of time that individuals spent sitting at a workstation by up to two hours more per day, yet, most workers indicated being as productive working remotely as compared to office work before the pandemic.[\[37\]](#cite_note-38) Supporting workers to identify effective approaches for boundary management between home and work across physical spaces, social interactions, and the use of time is critical.[\[38\]](#cite_note-39) Research suggests that remote work can lead to increased employee satisfaction and productivity, but may also create challenges in team cohesion.[\[39\]](#cite_note-40)

The transition to remote work during the pandemic highlighted the importance of access and equity among individual workers to support productivity and well-being. The remote work arrangement during COVID-19 was better for higher-paid and higher-management personnel in terms of productivity and reported well-being; whereas individuals at the bottom end of the earning spectrum experienced reduced remuneration.[\[40\]](#cite_note-41) Utility bills also increased during the COVID-19 pandemic in an inconsistent manner. Utility bills for minorities and lower income individuals were more likely to increase because they lived in housing that was older, with less effective [insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_insulation "Building insulation") and without [energy-efficient appliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efficient_energy_use#Appliances "Efficient energy use"). The increase in electricity also came due to the people using their utilities at different times of the day.[\[41\]](#cite_note-42)

A 2024 [PNAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNAS "PNAS") study found that remote work dispersed economic activity away from city centers, in particular in cities with high levels of remote work.[\[42\]](#cite_note-43)

### Communication technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Communication technology")\]

Effective group communication involves various nonverbal communication characteristics. Because distance limits interpersonal interaction between members of [distributed groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_team?action=edit&redlink=1 "Distributed team (page does not exist)"), these characteristics often become constrained. [Communication media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_media "Communication media") focuses on alternative ways to achieve these qualities and promote effective communication. This section addresses [communication technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication_technology "Communication technology") in relation to the theories of [grounding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_\(communication\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grounding (communication) (page does not exist)") and [mutual knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_knowledge "Common knowledge") and discusses the costs and benefits of various communication technology tools..

#### Grounding and technology

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Grounding and technology")\]

[Grounding in communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounding_in_communication "Grounding in communication") is the process of updating the evolving common ground, or shared information, between participants. The base of mutual knowledge is important for effective coordination and communication.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64) Additionally, participants constantly gather various forms of verbal and nonverbal evidence to establish understanding of change and task.

The following are means of grounding and collecting evidence:

Quality

Description

Co-presence

When sharing the same physical environment, participants are able to easily and hear what the other is doing and looking at.

Visibility

The participants are able to see each other and are able to pick up non-verbal facial cues and body language.

Audibility

When the participants are able to communicate by speaking, they are able to pick up voice intonation and utterance timing.

Cotemporality

Efficiency is promoted when an utterance is produced just about when it is received and understood, without delay.

Simultaneity

Messages can be simultaneously conveyed and received by both participants.

Sequentiality

The participants speak only with each other without intervening turns from conversations with other people.

Reviewability

Participants are able to return to a physical form of the exchange at a later time.

Revisability

Participants are able to privately revise their statements before sending their message.

Different forms of [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communication "Communication") result in the varied presence of these communication characteristics. Therefore, the nature of communication technology can either promote or inhibit grounding between participants. The absence of grounding information results in reduced ability to read and understand social cues. This increases the social distance between them.[\[60\]](#cite_note-:0a-64)

There is also often a [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation "Correlation") between the costs. ## Legal aspects

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legal aspects")\]

In 1996, the [Home Work Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Work_Convention "Home Work Convention"), an [International Labour Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Labour_Organization "International Labour Organization") (ILO) [Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty"), was created to offer protection to workers who are employed in their own homes.

The UK's [National Minimum Wage Act 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Minimum_Wage_Act_1998 "National Minimum Wage Act 1998") makes specific reference to home workers who "contract with a person, for the purposes of that person's business, for the execution of work to be done in a place not under the control or management of that person".[\[61\]](#cite_note-65) In the case of [James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_v_Redcats_\(Brands\)_Ltd "James v Redcats (Brands) Ltd") (2007), it was confirmed that "a home worker need not work at home, although typically he or she will do so; the only requirement is to work in a place not under the control or management of the other party".[\[62\]](#cite_note-66)

In the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), the Flexible Working Act allows workers to submit a written request to work from home, at least partly. Employers must have a good reason for refusing worker requests.[\[63\]](#cite_note-67)

## Potential benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Potential benefits")\]

### Disability employment

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Disability employment")\]

A 2026 study in the *[American Economic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Economic_Review "American Economic Review")* found that the expansion of remote work has led to a substantial increase in disability employment by reducing the commuting costs of physically disabled workers and allowing them to better control their work conditions to suit their disabilities.[\[64\]](#cite_note-aer2026-68)\[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*\]

### Access to more employees/employers

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Access to more employees/employers")\]

Remote work allows employees and employers to be matched despite major location differences.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

Working responsibility is given to the employee who is skilled in that area of work.[\[66\]](#cite_note-Hunter-2019-70)

### Cost reduction

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Cost reduction")\]

Remote work can [reduce costs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_reduction "Cost reduction") for organizations, including the cost of office space and related expenses such as parking, computer equipment, furniture, [office supplies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_supplies "Office supplies"), lighting and [heating, ventilation, and air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heating,_ventilation,_and_air_conditioning "Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning").[\[67\]](#cite_note-profits-71) Certain employee expenses, such as office expenses, can be shifted to the remote worker, although this is the subject of lawsuits.[\[68\]](#cite_note-72)

Remote work also reduces costs for the worker such as costs of travel/[commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting")[\[69\]](#cite_note-73)[\[70\]](#cite_note-impact-74) and clothing.[\[71\]](#cite_note-75) It also allows for the possibility of living in a cheaper area than that of the office.[\[65\]](#cite_note-masterclass-69)

### Environmental benefits

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environmental benefits")\]

See also: [Mobility transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobility_transition "Mobility transition")

Remote work can reduce [traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion "Traffic congestion") and [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution "Air pollution"), with fewer cars on the roads.

Most studies find that remote work overall results in a decrease in energy use due to less time spent on energy-intensive personal transportation,[\[72\]](#cite_note-76) cleaner air,[\[73\]](#cite_note-77) and a reduction of electricity usage due to a lower office space footprint.[\[74\]](#cite_note-78)

During the [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns"), the increase in remote work led to a decrease in global [CO2 emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CO2_emissions "CO2 emissions").[\[75\]](#cite_note-79) Partially due to the decrease in car commuting, carbon emissions dropped by 5.4%; however, emissions immediately increased to the same rate in the following year.[\[76\]](#cite_note-80)

The increase in remote work had also led to people moving out of cities and into larger homes which catered for home office space.[\[77\]](#cite_note-81)

### Fewer disruptions and distractions

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Remote_work&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Fewer disruptions and distractions")\]

Empirical studies find fewer in-office interruptions as a mechanism for productivity gains in remote or hybrid arrangements, particularly for knowledge-based work and concentration-heavy tasks. These include ambient noise such as background chatter and noise from machinery, and forced disruptions such as meetings and check-ins that an on-site employee would not have control over. Remote work gives employees flexibility and control over their environment in regard to distractions.

A 2024 study published by the *[Journal of Business and Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Business_and_Psychology "Journal of Business and Psychology")* found that there was a positive effect on daily job performance when working remotely, mediated by higher concentration and greater work engagement.[\[78\]](#cite_note-82) A 2025 study published by *[Computers in Human Behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computers_in_Human_Behavior "Computers in Human Behavior")* found that working from home increased job concentration; in particular, among those with stable personality traits, the negative effects of increased social isolation were buffered.[\[79\]](#cite_note-83)
